idiom_name: policy as a function or plain object passed into the host
implementation_notes: In JavaScript the policy unit is just a value: a plain object with the expected methods, a single function, or a map of functions, handed to the host's constructor or factory and stored in a field - there is no type-level binding at all, so interchangeability is the default and the classic host+policy-class structure collapses into composition plus a documented shape. Object assembly (or Object.assign/prototype copies for structural policies) replaces inheritance-based composition, and a @typedef/JSDoc contract or a one-time runtime check replaces the compile-time contract. The classic form is worth reconstructing only when a policy set is fixed once at start-up and the host sits on a hot path.
pitfalls: Nothing enforces the policy shape: a missing method fails only when called (a TypeError inside the host), so document the contract or validate it once in the constructor.
Policies are ordinary mutable objects shared by reference: mutating a policy after injection changes every host that holds it.

Every policy call is a dynamic property lookup, so this idiom cannot deliver the inline, zero-cost property of compile-time policies; extract hot policies into local variables when profiling demands it.
